headline: Most human communication is nonverbal—we speak volumes without saying a word
universal_truth: True understanding requires attention to what isn't said
fun_facts: Studies suggest 55% of communication is body language, 38% tone, and only 7% words
Micro-expressions—lasting just 1/25th of a second—can reveal hidden emotions
Humans can recognize a fake smile vs. a genuine smile by whether the eyes crinkle
discussion_questions: When has someone's body language told you more than their words?
How well do you think you read nonverbal cues?
What signals might you be sending without realizing?

hook.script: You say 'I'm fine' but your arms are crossed, your jaw is tight, and you won't make eye contact. Which message is true? Words are only part of communication—often the smaller part. We understand each other through channels we rarely notice.

cliff.script: If most communication is nonverbal, how do we decode it? How do we know what a gesture, expression, or tone actually means? And can we improve at reading these signals?
cliff.prompt: How do we interpret nonverbal communication?

options.text: We're born with some ability and learn the rest through experience and culture
options.response: Yes. Some basics are universal, but much is learned from our specific cultural environment.

options.text: Nonverbal cues are mostly universal across all humans
options.response: Some basics are universal, but many gestures vary by culture...

fact1.title: Beyond Words
fact1.script: Research suggests words carry only about 7% of emotional meaning. Tone of voice carries 38%. Body language carries 55%. We think we communicate with language, but our bodies are doing most of the talking.

fact2.title: Micro-Expressions
fact2.script: Micro-expressions are involuntary facial expressions lasting just fractions of a second. They can reveal emotions people are trying to hide. With training, you can learn to spot these flickers of truth that escape conscious control.

fact3.title: The Eyes Have It
fact3.script: A genuine smile—called a Duchenne smile—involves muscles around the eyes that are hard to control voluntarily. When someone really smiles, their eyes crinkle. A fake smile uses only the mouth. We detect the difference without knowing how.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: True understanding requires attention to what isn't said. Listen with your eyes. Watch for alignment between words and body. The complete message is always more than the words.

outro.script: That's Day 92. Tomorrow, we'll discover why humans have language. Until then, watch a conversation with the sound off—notice how much you understand anyway.

growTrack.title: Nonverbal Awareness - Read the Full Message
growTrack.activity: In your next conversation, consciously notice nonverbal signals: posture, eye contact, gestures, tone. Does the body match the words? What information comes through channels other than language?
